Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into what you saw in the outage and what you care about for runbook. Uh, Jordan, want to start?
[00:25] Jordan (Meridian): Yeah, thanks. Uh, hey Alex, Priya. So real quick context — Meridian runs a global customer support assistant, about 600 req/s at peak right now. We had two incidents in May, one zone-level and one control-plane blip that caused about 12 minutes of elevated errors. So we're exploring options to reduce blast radius and get predictable recovery behavior.
[01:05] Priya (Redwood SE): Got it. When you say control-plane blip, is that your own infra or a cloud provider event?
[01:12] Jordan: It was cloud provider; our sidecar infra also had some reconnect churn. During the incident our requests either timed out or retried and piled up. We want to avoid that cascade, ideally with automatic graceful degradation rather than blackouts.
[01:32] Sam (Meridian): And we care about consistent p99 latency, we can't have spikes over 6s, otherwise end users see timeouts and support tickets spike.
[01:42] Alex: Understood. A few quick clarifying q's — what's your tolerable error budget per month? Is a 0.1% error budget okay or tighter?
[01:54] Jordan: We're targeting 0.05% for now, but in practice we might accept short bursts if there's graceful degrade. The execs want SLAs for core flows; platform team is focused on availability.
[02:15] Priya: Cool. Can you share your current routing? Do you use active-active multi-region or active-passive? And DNS TTLs?
[02:24] Sam: Active-active across US-East and EU-West. DNS TTLs are pretty long, like 300s, which slowed us down in the last failover. We're exploring shorter TTLs and health-check-driven routing.
[02:38] Lena (SecOps): From security side, want to reiterate: keys must be in our KMS; audit logs retained for 2y; SSO via SAML and SCIM provisioning. Also we need SOC2 attestation and encryption in transit and at rest.
[02:56] Alex: Great, those are all supported options. On KMS: Redwood Private allows customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-KMS), Dedicated integrates with cloud KMS, and Hosted can work with envelope encryption but we'd need a KMS bridge. We'll share the exact docs.
[03:15] Priya: On the reliability strategies side, typically we present three escape hatches: 1) automatic model degrade — switch to a smaller model or use quantized variant under pressure; 2) warm standby region with prefix caching so KV cash (sic) is primed; 3) a queued backoff for non-real-time requests. Which of those sounds aligned?
[03:37] Jordan: Model degrade sounds promising if quality holds. But we need to measure re-ranking/answer quality to ensure user experience doesn't tank.
[03:45] Sam: Warm standby is also interesting. We don't want cold-start latencies when we flip region. How fast is prefix/KV cache warm-up in your system?
[03:55] Priya: Typically, with automatic prefix caching and a small warm set we can reach effective hit rates within a few minutes for top-k prefixes. But that depends on cache footprint and session stickiness. We also recommend continuous warmers for critical keys.
[04:12] Jordan: Continuous warmers, meaning you keep a small stream of synthetic traffic?
[04:16] Priya: Yeah, keep the KV cache primed. Also for large contexts the network transfer of KV cache between regions can be slow; better to pre-warm.
[04:27] Alex: Question on routing: do you prefer DNS failover, anycast, or an application-level router? Each has tradeoffs — DNS is simple but TTLs and DNS caching can delay failover; anycast provides fast failover but is more ops-heavy; app-level router gives finer control.
[04:43] Sam: We like finer control — our infra team wants a circuit-breaker at the edge that can route to a fallback, plus telemetry hooks.
[04:52] Priya: Redwood supports smart routing rules — can route by latency, by model variant, by customer tier. We also do automatic fallback to capacity tiers: e.g., route to dedicated pool or to a cheaper warm standby, depending on policy.
[05:06] Jordan: If we route to a cheaper model under load, do you preserve context? Like token-level continuity?
[05:14] Priya: Good question. If you switch to a quantized variant that's arch-compatible you'll maintain architectural continuity but output distribution might shift slightly. For chat continuity we recommend an orchestrated migration: keep context length limits similar and run A/B checks.
[05:30] Sam: Any data residency implications when failing over to another region? EU customers must remain in EU region, so failover may not be allowed for some traffic.
[05:38] Alex: Right — routing policies can be scoped per-customer or per-route; you can pin EU users to EU-only fallback policies. We'll document policy examples.
[05:51] Jordan: On SLA language, execs ask for a 99.95% uptime for core flows. How does Redwood's Dedicated SLA compare?
[05:59] Alex: Dedicated has SLA tiers; 99.95% is on the table for reserved capacity with specific anti-affinity and redundancy. Hosted SLA is more conservative, but you get faster time to market. We can share the exact contract language.
[06:15] Lena: Also need to confirm audit trails: every inference request must be logged with request id, model version, and user id (PII redaction rules apply). Is that supported?
[06:25] Priya: Yes — per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdowns exist. For hosted we can stream logs to your Splunk/Datadog; for Private you run locally. Redaction is pluggable at the ingestion point.
[06:40] Jordan: Curious about incident scenarios: what happens if a single GPU node OOMs in Dedicated? Do you have automatic draining and reroute?
[06:50] Priya: We have node-level health checks and autoscaler drains; traffic routed off a draining node to available replicas. If capacity is low, the system can either queue or degrade. We recommend a buffer of reserved capacity to handle node failures.
[07:05] Sam: How long to recover from region-wide outage in your experience? Realistically, between detection and traffic normalization?
[07:14] Alex: Depends on routing policy and whether you pre-warm standby. With pre-warmed standby and short DNS TTLs, recovery can be under 90s for routing changes; if you're relying on DNS alone and caches, it could be minutes.
[07:28] Jordan: Hmm, 90s would be great. In the May outage we had 12 minutes — partly due to TTLs and some config drift.
[07:36] Priya: We also provide health-check probes that can do active golden-traffic tests. Those can trigger automated route shifts faster than DNS TTL expiry.
[07:46] Lena: About compliance: we need to see SOC2 plus encryption key lifecycle docs. Also want to know if Redwood supports HSM for private deployments.
[07:56] Alex: Yes HSM/KMS supported for Private. For Dedicated we integrate with cloud KMS and can provide attestations. We'll attach the compliance pack.
[08:07] Sam: Any limitations on model size or quantization when using Dedicated vs Hosted?
[08:13] Priya: Dedicated gives more flexibility on larger unquantized models and custom kernels; Hosted catalog is curated but includes several large options — there are tradeoffs with unit-cost. We can show cost versus latency curves.
[08:28] Jordan: Can you run a quick scenario: if US-East had a partial outage, how would traffic flow with a recommended policy?
[08:36] Priya: Typically: detect via health probes, mark node unhealthy; edge circuit-breaker redirects to warm standby region for affected routes; for latency-sensitive flows we route to a quantized local fall-back; non-critical flows get queued to be processed later. We'll also emit alerts and execute an incident runbook.
[08:56] Alex: We'll include a sample runbook — detection, mitigation steps, manual escalation, rollback to previous model, and post-incident RCA responsibilities.
[09:05] Jordan: Important: we expect to run internal drills — game days. Can you support synthetic golden-traffic and inject faults for tabletop exercises?
[09:14] Priya: Yes, we support synthetic traffic tooling and can run tabletop scenarios with your SREs. We can also share our incident playbooks for graceful degradation.
[09:27] Sam: A couple of engineering nits — what telemetry do you export? We want spans, metrics, and the ability to trace a request from edge to model output.
[09:36] Alex: We export traces and metrics; you can integrate with OpenTelemetry. Request ids and model-version meta are included.
[09:44] Lena: Also need role-based access and audit logs for who changed routing policies or model rollouts.
[09:51] Priya: RBAC and audit trail for rollout events exist. For Private we can integrate with your IAM; for Hosted we have a tenant admin console with audit logs.
[10:02] Jordan: Pricing question — how do you price dedicated pools vs hosted burst? If we reserve an 8xA100 pool, what's the ballpark?
[10:10] Alex: We'll give a committed monthly number — for an 8xA100 pool expect a committed rate plus an overage burst price. I'll get you a preliminary quote; pricing depends on SLA band and support tier.
[10:21] Sam: For our PoC, we might start on Hosted with canary traffic, then move to Dedicated if it proves stable. Is that a common path?
[10:29] Priya: Very common. Start hosted for fast iteration, move to Dedicated when you need predictable performance and stricter controls.
[10:36] Jordan: Okay, two technical follow-ups — 1) can you run a p99 latency test with our real trace? 2) show behavior of fallback to warm standby under synthetic failover?
[10:46] Alex: Yup, we'll run both. Please upload a sanitized trace and we'll run it against a hosted baseline and a dedicated baseline.
[10:54] Lena: Also ask about patching windows and maintenance: do maintenance events affect SLA? What notification cadence?
[11:03] Alex: Maintenance windows are communicated; for Dedicated reserved capacity we schedule with you and minimize impact. Hosted maintenance may have short degraded windows but are part of the SLA terms.
[11:17] Sam: One ops detail — how do you handle model rollbacks if a new model causes quality regressions? Can you A/B and do automatic rollback?
[11:26] Priya: Yes — rollouts support canary, A/B, and automatic rollback based on quality metrics or error thresholds. We can tie rollouts to eval suites so regressions trigger rollbacks.
[11:38] Jordan: We saw some model drift last quarter, so we want automatic regression detection. Good to know.
[11:45] Alex: On contracts, for Private deployments we do an enterprise license with support and a longer onboarding window. For Dedicated it's a reserved capacity contract with monthly/annual commit. We'll send examples.
[11:58] Sam: How does data residency work for backups and logs? We need backups to stay in regional storage.
[12:06] Priya: Backup location can be configured; for Private it's under your control, for Dedicated we can pin backups to region with encryption at rest.
[12:16] Jordan: Any known gotchas on network egress costs when failing over across regions?
[12:22] Alex: Yes egress is a cost factor. We'll include an estimate for cross-region replication and warm-standby sync traffic.
[12:33] Lena: Security question — can we run in air-gapped mode for a subset of consumers?
[12:38] Priya: For highly regulated customers Private on-prem package can be air-gapped; we'll discuss deployment topology for that.
[12:47] Sam: About observability retention — we might need 90 days for traces and 2 years for audit events. Is that an add-on?
[12:55] Alex: Longer retention is an add-on; it can be part of enterprise package.
[13:02] Jordan: Let's talk toleration windows for model degrade — how long can degrade mode be kept before execs escalate?
[13:10] Lena: Execs want a manual review at 15 minutes of degraded UX.
[13:14] Sam: So automated degrade could run for short bursts, but after 15 minutes trigger human intervention.
[13:21] Priya: We can configure auto-degrade thresholds and escalation policies. Good to codify that in the runbook.
[13:29] Alex: Quick note: competitors like BigCloudAI often emphasize single-region large fleets; InferX sells self-hosted runtime but lacks the integrated rollout tooling. Reducing vendor lock and having consistent API across Hosted/Dedicated/Private is a Redwood differentiator.
[13:49] Jordan: Pricing and security pack will be the deciding factors. Also need to see a reference architecture for warm standby.
[13:58] Alex: We'll attach an architecture doc with sample warm-standby sync patterns and a suggested SLO table showing p50/p95/p99 targets and recommended error budgets.
[14:10] Sam: One last engineering detail — how do you handle session affinity when routing across regions? We need sticky sessions for continuity.
[14:18] Priya: We support session affinity at the edge and sticky tokens. If you route across regions we can propagate session context, but with caveats for data residency.
[14:28] Jordan: Ok that's a lot, but super helpful. Any last asks from your side?
[14:33] Alex: Upload sanitized traces, the incidents' postmortem, and your current routing config. We'll use those to run the test.
[14:41] Jordan: Will do.
[14:44] Alex: Cool. Recap and next steps: 1) Redwood to send SOC2 / KMS / HSM docs and compliance pack; 2) Redwood to run benchmarks with provided trace; 3) schedule infra deep-dive week of Jun 22; 4) provide preliminary Dedicated pricing.
[15:02] Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks both.

End of meeting.
